analysis.title: Gigawatts vs. Bragawatts: 586GW Announced, 199 Real - Mapping Who Is Actually Building America's Data Centers
key_insights: Bernstein's October refresh ran all 8,858 North American projects in the Aterio database through a credibility model and probability-weighted the 5,697 that remain. Of 586 GW under construction, announced or land-banked, 199 GW (34%) is credible and 387 GW is not.

The haircuts in the waterfall: stage of development removes 198 GW, tenant quality 113 GW, developer track record 48 GW, state politics 28 GW. The state-politics haircut that Wall Street has been modeling since the election is the smallest of the four.
The credible share has stayed near 33% (first run), 35% (August) and 34% (now) while the pipeline grew from 411 GW to 586 GW. Of the 98 GW added since August, Bernstein credits 29 GW.

Base probabilities: 90-98% for projects under construction, 50% for announced-only projects from a third-party developer, 25% for land merely owned. Announced projects are 497 GW (85% of the pipeline) and Bernstein expects about a quarter of them to happen. Projects under construction are 87 GW and 86% credible, so the 15% of the pipeline under construction becomes 38% of what gets built.

The US has about 58 GW of data centers operating. The 75 GW of credible capacity under construction would more than double that, and the full 199 GW is 3.4x current capacity. Bernstein's June note called this a 5-10 year build.

Hyperscalers building for themselves and established colocation operators are 37% of announced GW and 76% of credible GW. The 'Others' bucket announced 308 GW (over half the pipeline) and Bernstein expects 33 GW (11%) to be built. Miner pivots score 24% and neoclouds 29%.

Bernstein scores developers 0-5 on power path (35% weight), capital (30%), offtake (25%) and execution (10%). Sixteen score 5.0. Developers at 4-5 see 68% of their pipeline survive. Those at 0-1 announced 142 GW (about a quarter of the national total) and are credited with 7 GW (5%).
Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta account for 78 GW, about 39% of credible capacity. The top ten developers account for about 57%.

O'Leary Ventures announced 15.0 GW across 110 projects (7.5 GW at Wonder Valley in Alberta, 7.5 GW at 'Stratos' in Box Elder County, Utah), all announced-only. Bernstein credits 489 MW (3.3%) and gives it the database's lowest credibility score, 0.35 of 5. Joule Capital Partners has 11.7 GW across 50 projects on one Utah campus, with a $60M Series B and no anchor tenant. Bernstein credits 1.1 GW.

Vermaland's $33B La Osa megasite near Eloy, Arizona was cut from 3 GW to 1 GW and rejected 4-1 by Pinal County supervisors on August 26. Bernstein's model gave it a 4% survival rate, and the outcome was zero.

Private builders: QTS has 11.5 GW credible of 14.3 GW (80%) and is carrying 1.6 GW of cancellations after exiting the Prince William Digital Gateway in July. Vantage has 7.2 GW of 9.0 GW (80%, 40% of its book under construction). STACK has 7.7 GW of 11.1 GW (69%).

Tenant multipliers: Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Nvidia 1.00. OpenAI alone 0.50 (equal to Groq), trimmed after OpenAI cut its funding round target to $20B from roughly $30B. Oracle cut to 0.75 from 0.80 after the Project Jupiter force majeure notice and Moody's negative outlook. Oracle/OpenAI 0.80 from 0.85. CoreWeave, Nebius and Lambda 0.45. xAI 0.60. Jane Street and Bloomberg 0.80. Microsoft plus OpenAI 0.95. Nscale 0.40 alone and 0.80 with Microsoft.

Hyperscaler self-build is about 41% (82 GW) of credible capacity. AWS leads named third-party tenants with 9.2 GW credible, and OpenAI-linked demand is second at 5.8 GW, with Vantage, Related Digital, BorderPlex and Crusoe building for Oracle/OpenAI.

Developer-side changes: Crusoe, Sabey and Serverfarm were upgraded on new financing. Nscale was downgraded after Microsoft's exit and Fermi America after its TensorWave lease failed to close. Capital is getting easier and offtake harder.

State haircut: 68% of credible pipeline sits in 13 states Bernstein flags as risky. Texas and Pennsylvania join Virginia and New York at a 0.70 floor. Georgia and Ohio are at 0.80. Maryland and Louisiana are new to the table. Projects under construction are treated as grandfathered.

Texas has 150 GW in the database, about 43 GW credible (22% of the national credible total), and a roughly 12 GW state haircut, twice Virginia's. 21 GW is under construction and grandfathered. By year: 2027 has 11 GW nameplate and 0.3 GW credible, 2028 has 18 GW announced and 5 GW credible (most at risk), 2029 has 39 GW and 8 GW. Bernstein frames the Texas pause under Governor-elect Hinojosa as delay more than cancellation risk.

JPMorgan's Cembalest: 2027 is safe (75% of 37 GW due is under construction). Of 96 GW expected in 2028, 37.5 GW is in states where the winner wants a pause and 15 GW where the winner wants conditions, so 55% of 2028 faces new restrictions, with Texas at 26.5 GW. JPMorgan's 96 GW for 2028 is nearly four times Morgan Stanley's 25 GW expected to switch on that year and above Bernstein's 75 GW of credible capacity under construction nationally.

Georgia's Public Service Commission flipped 3-2 Democratic. Major approvals (including OpenAI's 3.2 GW contract) are done, so the leverage is over Georgia Power's next capacity request and 2028 rate case. 87% of the state's pre-construction credible capacity is dated 2029 or later, so Georgia gets more expensive later, without much added near-term risk.

Ohio: a quick read suggested about 3 GW of credible capacity zoned out, but Bernstein finds the bans bind on about 1.1 GW because AWS's 1.5 GW Trenton campus is outside the city line. On November 10 the Butler County Planning Commission unanimously recommended approval of a ban in St. Clair Township. If the township adopts it, about 1 GW of AWS credible capacity becomes binding, roughly doubling Ohio's total. Local bans bite faster than state action, and projects tend to move to the next town.

Behind-the-meter (BTM) pipeline grew 22.5 GW in October to 231 GW and was 48% of October additions. Only 4% of operating capacity uses on-site power, versus 17% of capacity under construction and 43% of announced. The BTM pipeline grew 46 GW since August while credible BTM rose about 5 GW to 47 GW. Only 0.2 GW of BTM broke ground in October.

BTM share by developer: neoclouds 62% of pipeline, 'Others' 54%, hyperscalers 19%. Credible share of BTM: hyperscalers 73%, neoclouds 21%, 'Others' 10% (167 GW of the 231 GW). BTM is 28% of stranded capacity, up from 16% in May. October's largest addition was Valar Atomics' 9.6 GW nuclear-powered 'Project Beehive' in Utah, and its largest cancellation was the 4.0 GW DCIP campus in De Soto, Florida. SoftBank wrote off $3.7B of prepaid power-generation equipment on Tuesday.

Geography: a gigawatt costs $12-15B and waits 4-7 years for power in major metros, versus $7-9B and 1-3 years in rural areas. Emerging and rural markets hold 398 GW (about 70% of the pipeline) and have a 31% modeled build probability versus about 40% in metros. Bernstein prefers incumbents with the most credible pipelines and has an Underperform on CoreWeave.

Zero Hedge's own math: at Bernstein's $7-15B per GW (and its own estimate of about $49B all-in per GW), 387 GW of non-credible capacity is $3-6 trillion of buildings and roughly $19 trillion of total spending that exists only in announcements. The author expects the 34% credible share to fall because the tenant haircut is already four times the political one.

Zero Hedge attributes the political backlash partly to inflated announcements: ERCOT's 474 GW queue prompted Abbott's audit and the August Texas pause, and data centers were on 45 ballots last week, losing 44.

market_movers.rationale: Bernstein keeps an Underperform. Neoclouds get a 0.45 tenant multiplier, 62% of their pipeline is behind the meter, and only 21% of that is credible.
Bernstein cut Oracle's tenant multiplier to 0.75 from 0.80, and the Oracle/OpenAI pairing to 0.80 from 0.85, after the Project Jupiter force majeure notice and Moody's negative outlook.
Nebius carries a 0.45 tenant multiplier, below xAI at 0.60 and Jane Street and Bloomberg at 0.80.
A Microsoft lease carries a 1.00 multiplier, and Microsoft plus OpenAI is 0.95. Microsoft also exited Nscale's Loughton site.
Equinix is among the 16 developers with a perfect 5.0 developer score, and Bernstein prefers incumbents with the most credible pipelines.
Digital Realty is among the 16 developers with a perfect 5.0 developer score, and Bernstein prefers incumbents with the most credible pipelines.
Brookfield is among the 16 developers with a perfect 5.0 developer score, and Bernstein prefers incumbents with the most credible pipelines.

risk_factors: Tenant credit: the tenant haircut (113 GW) is about four times the political haircut (28 GW). OpenAI alone scores 0.50 and is the second-largest named third-party customer (5.8 GW credible).
Oracle credit and the Oracle/OpenAI pairing used for Stargate, following the Project Jupiter force majeure notice and Moody's negative outlook.
State moratoria and conditions, concentrated in Texas (about 12 GW state haircut), Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, Georgia and Ohio.
Local zoning bans move faster than state action, though projects often relocate to the next town.
Behind-the-meter projects are the least likely to be built and make up 28% of stranded capacity.
Cancellations and tenant exits, such as Microsoft leaving Nscale's Loughton site, a failed TensorWave lease at Fermi America and QTS's 1.6 GW of cancellations.
Zero Hedge expects the 34% credible share to fall. The author also warns that spending forecasts built on announced capacity may rest on projects that will not be built.
geopolitical: US state politics: Democratic governors elected last Tuesday and state moratorium proposals, with Texas and Pennsylvania joining Virginia and New York at Bernstein's 0.70 floor and Georgia and Ohio at 0.80.

Texas Governor-elect Hinojosa has backed a pause on data center approvals until the Legislature acts, with a Democratic House and a Republican Senate. Both candidates wanted the sales-tax exemption removed.
Georgia Public Service Commission flipped 3-2 Democratic.
Local zoning bans in Ohio, including the St. Clair Township proposal in Butler County.
Data centers were on 45 ballot measures last week and lost 44, per the author.
Arizona's Pinal County supervisors rejected the La Osa rezoning 4-1 on August 26.
cross_bank_references: Goldman says state moratoria could hit about 45% of planned US capacity.
Barclays found that 80% of the roughly 300 GW 'high probability' pipeline will sit in states with a Democratic governor next year.
Morgan Stanley sized Texas and Ohio at 12 GW through 2030 and flagged 4.9 GW for 2028, and expects 25 GW to switch on in 2028.
JPMorgan's Cembalest counted 52.5 GW of 2028 capacity in states whose next governor wants a pause or new conditions.
Wood Mackenzie concluded in August that more than two-thirds of the power sought for US data centers will never materialize.
Goldman expects behind-the-meter generation to supply 25% of all data centers by 2030.

tension_points.bull_case: Bernstein says the credible pipeline keeps growing (136 GW, then 170 GW, now 199 GW). The best builders are the least exposed and politics will delay more than kill projects. Hyperscalers and established colos hold 76% of credible capacity.
tension_points.bear_case: About two-thirds of each new batch of announcements is discarded. The tenant haircut (113 GW) is about four times the political one (28 GW), OpenAI alone scores 0.50 and Oracle's multiplier fell for a second update. Zero Hedge expects the 34% credible share to fall.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further cuts to tenant multipliers, such as OpenAI's funding or Oracle's credit worsening, would lower the 34% credible share.

tension_points.bull_case: Bernstein sees delay more than cancellation: 21 GW is under construction and grandfathered, tax incentives remain, and much of the 2028 capacity was likely to be late anyway.
tension_points.bear_case: Governor-elect Hinojosa wants a pause until the Legislature acts, and both candidates wanted the sales-tax exemption removed. JPMorgan counts 26.5 GW of 2028 Texas capacity facing new restrictions.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Repeal of the sales-tax exemption or a prolonged legislative standoff would deepen the pause.

tension_points.bull_case: The BTM pipeline reached 231 GW, 48% of October additions, and Goldman expects BTM to supply 25% of data centers by 2030.
tension_points.bear_case: Only 4% of operating capacity uses on-site power, credible BTM is 47 GW, only 0.2 GW broke ground in October, and BTM is 28% of stranded capacity.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sustained rise in BTM capacity breaking ground, such as well above the 0.2 GW seen in October, would undercut the bear case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Only 34% of the 586 GW pipeline is credible, and the ratio has stayed flat as the pipeline grew.
OpenAI alone is scored a 50/50 credit and Oracle's multiplier was cut for a second update.
theme_stances.evidence: OpenAI on its own gets 0.50, the same as Groq

theme_stances.key_argument: Bernstein frames the Texas pause as delay more than cancellation risk, with 2028 capacity most at risk.
BTM is the least likely to be built and the share of stranded capacity is rising.
theme_stances.evidence: Almost none of it is real yet.
